title: Emraan Hashmi Walks Back Into the Dark. After Five Years, the King of Bollywood Horror Returns — With a Soundtrack.
excerpt: 'Rooh' reunites the genre's most recognisable face with the 'Breathe' director for a big-screen musical-horror spectacle, releasing pan-India in 2027.
body:
The man who taught a generation to be afraid of the dark is walking back into it. After five years away from the genre that made him a household name, Emraan Hashmi is returning to horror — and this time he's bringing a soundtrack.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=HQBxZjXSm5c

On Tuesday morning, Vicked Films dropped the title announcement for Rooh, a self-described "musical-horror spectacle" built, deliberately and defiantly, for the big screen. No streaming hedge, no quiet OTT drop. This one wants you in a dark theatre with the sound turned all the way up. The film is slated for a 2027 release in Hindi, Tamil and Telugu — a pan-India swing that tells you exactly how big the ambition is.

"Rooh is a film that immediately connected with me because it brings together new-age horror, emotion and music in a very powerful way."**
"Rooh is a film that immediately connected with me because it brings together new-age horror, emotion and music in a very powerful way. This is a space that audiences have always associated with me." — Emraan Hashmi

He's not wrong about that association. For the better part of two decades, Hashmi was Bollywood horror's leading man — the brooding centre of the Raaz films, the haunted houses, the things that go bump in the second half. There was a stretch where you couldn't walk past a multiplet poster without finding him staring out of some candlelit corridor, eyes wide, secret buried. Then he drifted: anti-hero turns, OTT thrillers, the villain in Tiger 3. The scares went quiet. Now they're back, and the timing feels almost too neat — Indian horror is having its loudest commercial moment in years, and the one star most synonymous with the genre had been sitting it out.

The most intriguing name in the announcement isn't even on screen. Rooh is directed by Mayank Sharma, the creator-director behind Prime Video's acclaimed Breathe franchise — a man who built his reputation on psychological dread, slow-burn menace and characters who unravel from the inside. Pairing that sensibility with Hashmi's instinct for atmosphere is a genuinely interesting bet. Breathe was never about cheap jolts; it was about the creeping certainty that something is wrong. Apply that to a full-blown theatrical horror film and you have something that could actually scare adults, not just startle them.

The screenplay comes from Sharma and Vishal Kapoor, the writer behind Lapachhapi and Chhorii — both films that understood horror works best when it's rooted in something real, usually maternal, usually grief. That pedigree matters. The Indian horror that travels — the kind the diaspora actually seeks out on a Friday night in New Jersey or Southall — tends to be the kind that's about something underneath the screaming. Rooh is produced by Vikram Khakhar and Sunny Khanna under Vicked Films Productions.

The "musical" part is the wild card. Horror and song are not natural roommates — done badly, a music number can puncture every ounce of tension a film has spent an hour building. But done well, it's hypnotic; think of the way a haunting melody can do more damage than a jump scare ever could. Hashmi's horror films were always quietly defined by their music — those Raaz tracks lived on long after the films faded. If Rooh can weave the songs into the fear rather than pausing the fear for them, it could carve out something genuinely new in a genre that's gotten comfortable cross-breeding with comedy.

And that's the quiet provocation here. So much of recent Indian horror — the Stree universe, Bhediya, the endless "horror-comedy" pipeline — has leaned on laughs as a safety net. Rooh is positioning itself as the opposite: serious, atmospheric, emotional, scary. A film that wants to make you feel something other than amused. After years of bhoots played for giggles, a straight-faced, big-screen, music-laced ghost story feels almost radical.

For the diaspora, the pan-India, three-language rollout is the headline. A 2027 theatrical release in Hindi, Tamil and Telugu means Rooh is being built for the same global desi audiences who turned recent South releases into international events — expect day-one screenings across the US, UK, Canada and the Gulf when it lands.

It's a long wait. But Emraan Hashmi in a dark theatre, a Breathe director behind the camera, and a Chhorii writer on the page is the most promising horror package Bollywood has assembled in a while. The dark has its old king back. Now we find out if he still knows how to make us flinch.
